newsitem.title: USA: Florida free to claim punitive tobacco damages.
newsitem.headline: Florida free to claim punitive tobacco damages.

text.p: U.S. cigarette companies said on Friday they had dropped pre-trial opposition to punitive claims by the State of Florida in a lawsuit seeking billions of dollars in state spending on sick people afflicted with smoking-related ailments.

A lawyer for Philip Morris Cos Inc, one of the defending tobacco companies, said in a news release that dropping pre-trial opposition had no legal effect and that the industry had never paid punitive damages in any lawsuit.

Florida is seeking $1 billion or more from U.S. cigarette makers for actual costs incurred in its Medicaid healthcare program. Punitive damages, assuming a victory for the state, would raise the potential losses to the industry substantially.

The state last month won the right to claim even further damages under Florida's anti-rackeetering laws, a precedent in the spreading legal battle against tobacco companies. State lawyers have said the racketeering claims could cost cigarette makers tens of billions of dollars.
The judge in the Florida trial, which is scheduled to begin in August in West Palm Beach, last fall threw out 15 of the state government's original 18 claims.

Gregory Little, lawyer for Philip Morris, said a key reason for the industry's decision was a worry that the state's lawyers would present evidence against cigarette makers during a public, pre-trial hearing which tobacco lawyers would be barred from defending against at that time.
"The lawyers for the state of Florida have demonstrated a remarkable propensity for trying their case in the media," Little said.
Such actions pollute the pool of potential jurors and make a fair trial more difficult, Little contended.

Defendants in the case, one of several such lawsuits brought by state governments scheduled to go to trial this year, include RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp and the Brown & Williamson unit of B.A.T Industries Plc.
